rationale.intervention_reconstruction: The hypothesis proposes a Ni coating on W particles followed by Cu infiltration, whereas the paper uses liquid-metal dealloying of a WTaVTi RHEA precursor in molten Cu to create a bicontinuous RHEA–Cu composite. These are fundamentally different kinds of interventions.
rationale.condition_agreement: The hypothesis mentions sintering/infiltration at ~1200 °C under inert atmosphere and irradiation testing, while the paper uses liquid-metal dealloying at 1200 °C for 96 h in vacuum-sealed silica, thermal conductivity measurement up to ~800 °C, and 25 keV He+ irradiation. The temperature and inert/vacuum environment are broadly similar, but the core processing step (infiltration vs. dealloying) and irradiation specifics differ.
rationale.mechanism_agreement: The hypothesis invokes improved wetting and diffusion bonding via a Ni interlayer to reduce voids, whereas the paper's mechanism relies on selective Ti dissolution from interdendritic channels, formation of a W-rich passivating interlayer, and aligned Cu channels for conductivity. These are different classes of mechanism.
rationale.outcome_agreement: The hypothesis predicts reduced voids and improved thermal conductivity relative to vapor-coated W–Cu composites, while the paper predicts and measures substantially increased thermal conductivity (surpassing pure W above ~650 °C) and reduced He-induced swelling relative to pure W. Both predict improved thermal conductivity, but the specific property direction and comparison baselines differ.
